sentences.text: Most individuals of this genus measured approximately 1.3 meters in length, although one large specimen reached 2.4 meters.
The premaxilla of the species A. scagliai featured a shovel-shaped tip that lacked the prominent lateral expansion seen in other relatives.
Histological analysis of a large specimen suggests it lived to be 23 years old.
The genus Aetosauroides was first described by Casamiquela in 1960.
Fossils have been recovered from northwestern Argentina and southeastern Brazil.
Although the animal possessed teeth resembling those of carnivores, its shovel-shaped snout and toothless jaw tips indicate an omnivorous diet.
One pathological specimen displays bone changes consistent with periostitis, likely resulting from non-traumatic stress followed by a pyogenic infection.
Aetosauroides was proposed to be synonymous with the genus Stagonolepis in 1996 and 2002, but this synonymy is not accepted.
A 2012 phylogenetic analysis found that Aetosauroides lies outside the family Stagonolepididae.
A 2011 study proposed that the species A. subsulcatus and A. inhamandensis are synonymous with the type species A. scagliai.
Two 2021 studies proposed that Polesinesuchus aurelioi is a junior synonym of Aetosauroides based on similarities in juvenile vertebrae and braincase structures.
Aetosauroides is one of four known aetosaur genera from South America.
The time range for Aetosauroides is estimated from 237 to 227.3 million years ago.
Researchers have suggested that sexual dimorphism exists in Aetosauroides, with males potentially reaching 2 meters in length.
